blocks.text: In the early 20th century Darwinism was combined with modern genetics to form Neo-Darwinism. In Neo-Darwinism evolution is defined more precisely as 'a change in the frequency of alleles in a population, or in the total genetic makeup of a population (the gene pool)'. Neo-Darwinism is based on the Hardy-Weinberg theorem.

blocks.title: For information: gene pool and frequencies
blocks.text: Gene pool: all the genes for a trait in a population; for example 1000 genes for flower colour. Allele frequency: the proportion of a particular allele; if 600 of the 1000 are for red, the frequency of red is 0.6 (60%). Genotype frequency: the proportion of individuals with a genotype; if 40 of 100 plants are RR, the RR frequency is 0.4 (40%).

In 1908 the English mathematician Godfrey Hardy and the German physician Wilhelm Weinberg stated that the frequencies of alleles and genotypes in a large, randomly mating population remain constant from generation to generation if no evolutionary forces act. If any of the following conditions is not met, evolution takes place.

items: Mating must be random: every individual has an equal chance of mating with any other.
No individuals migrate into or out of the population.
No mutations occur, or mutations from the wild-type allele to the mutant equal those back to the wild type.
All genotypes have an equal chance of survival and reproduction.

blocks.text: Genetic drift, often called neutral selection: chance events change gene frequencies, not fitness, and the effect is most obvious in small populations. For example, a fire reduces a population of 100 rabbits to 10, and the survivors happen to be mostly brown, so the new population has lower genetic diversity.

items: Gene flow: individuals entering (immigration) or leaving (emigration) a population change its gene frequencies; immigrants can bring in new alleles at once.

Mutation: mutations are the origin of all new genes and a source of variation that may prove adaptive, helping groups survive environmental shocks. Most are harmful; some are neutral, or harmful in one environment and useful in another. Mutational equilibrium, when forward and back mutations balance, rarely exists; mutation pressure measures the tendency of gene frequencies to change through mutation.
